q: Complete the peering settings for requirement 1.
tpl: On the hub-to-spoke peerings, enable [[0]]. On the spoke-to-hub peerings, enable [[1]].
exp: The hub shares its gateway with Allow gateway transit, and each spoke uses it with Use remote gateways.

q: What meets requirement 2?
opts: Peer VNet-App directly with VNet-Data
Add route tables to the spoke subnets that send the other spoke's prefix to the next hop type Virtual appliance at 10.0.1.4
Enable a service endpoint on both spokes
Add NSG rules that allow VNet-App to VNet-Data
exp: Peering is not transitive, and a direct peering would bypass the firewall. User-defined routes force spoke-to-spoke traffic through the firewall in the hub.

q: What meets requirement 3 with the least management effort?
opts: A jump box VM with a public IP in the hub
Azure Bastion in the hub VNet, which can reach VMs in peered spokes
A public IP on each VM, with RDP allowed only from the office
Point-to-site VPN for every administrator
exp: Azure Bastion provides browser-based RDP and SSH over TLS without public IPs on the VMs, and it works across VNet peering.

q: What meets requirement 4?
opts: A service endpoint for Microsoft.Sql on the spoke subnets
A private endpoint for the SQL server, a privatelink private DNS zone, and DNS forwarding for on-premises clients
An NSG rule allowing TCP 1433 from on-premises
A public endpoint restricted to the on-premises public IP
exp: Private endpoints give the SQL server a private IP that on-premises clients can reach over VPN. Service endpoints do not work from on-premises.

q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: The web VMs need an NSG rule that allows TCP 443, because the Standard load balancer is secure by default
VNet-App can reach VNet-Data through the hub peerings without any routes
The hub's Azure Firewall subnet can have any name
A spoke that uses the hub's gateway (Use remote gateways) can also have its own VPN gateway
exp: Standard load balancers need NSG rules to admit traffic. Peering is not transitive. Azure Firewall needs a subnet named AzureFirewallSubnet. A VNet that uses remote gateways cannot have its own gateway.

q: What must you do at the registrar for requirement 1?
opts: Create an A record that points to Azure
Replace the domain's NS records with the four Azure DNS name servers of the proseware.com zone
Add a TXT record with the Azure subscription ID
Nothing; Azure DNS takes over automatically
exp: Delegation works by setting the domain's name servers at the registrar to the Azure DNS name servers assigned to your zone.

q: Which record meets requirement 2?
opts: A CNAME record at the apex pointing to the load balancer
An alias A record at the apex that targets the load balancer's public IP resource
A static A record with the current IP address
An MX record
exp: CNAME records are not allowed at the zone apex. An alias record points at the Azure resource and follows its IP address automatically.

q: Complete the plan for requirement 3.
tpl: Create a [[0]] DNS zone named corp.proseware.internal, and link it to the VNet with [[1]] enabled.
exp: A private DNS zone resolves names inside linked VNets. Auto-registration creates and updates A records for the VMs.

q: What meets requirement 4?
opts: A public Standard load balancer with a rule for TCP 8443
An internal Standard load balancer with a private frontend IP and a rule for TCP 8443
An Application Gateway with a public listener
Traffic Manager with two endpoints
exp: An internal load balancer has a private frontend that only the VNet and connected networks can reach. It handles any TCP port.

q: What meets requirement 5?
opts: A load-balancing rule from port 50001 to port 3389
An inbound NAT rule from frontend port 50001 to VM 1 on port 3389
An outbound rule
Floating IP on the HTTPS rule
exp: Inbound NAT rules forward a frontend port to one specific backend VM. Load-balancing rules spread traffic across the pool.

q: Complete the command so the rule is evaluated before an existing custom Deny-All rule at priority 300 and allows HTTPS from the internet.
tpl:
az network nsg rule create -g RG1 --nsg-name nsg-web -n allow-https \
  --priority [[0]] --direction Inbound --access Allow --protocol Tcp \
  --destination-port-ranges 443 --source-address-prefixes [[1]]
exp: Lower numbers are evaluated first, so 200 comes before 300. Custom priorities run from 100 to 4096. The Internet service tag represents addresses outside the VNet.

q: Complete the route so all internet-bound traffic goes through the firewall at 10.0.1.4.
tpl:
az network route-table route create -g RG1 --route-table-name rt-spoke -n to-fw \
  --address-prefix 0.0.0.0/0 --next-hop-type [[0]] --next-hop-ip-address 10.0.1.4
exp: VirtualAppliance sends traffic to the IP address given. None would drop it, and Internet would bypass the firewall.

q: Complete the statement about the subnet 10.0.2.0/28.
tpl: The subnet has [[0]] usable addresses, and the first VM deployed in it gets [[1]].
exp: A /28 has 16 addresses; Azure reserves 5 (.0, .1, .2, .3 and .15), leaving 11. The first usable address is .4.

q: Complete the statement about Azure Bastion.
tpl: Azure Bastion (Basic or Standard) needs a subnet named [[0]] with a prefix of [[1]] or larger.
exp: Azure Bastion (Basic, Standard and Premium) must be deployed into a dedicated subnet named exactly AzureBastionSubnet, and the subnet must be /26 or larger so Bastion can scale. A smaller prefix such as /27 or a different name makes the deployment fail.

q: Complete the command for the hub side of a peering, so spokes can use the hub's VPN gateway.
tpl:
az network vnet peering create -g RG1 -n hub-to-app \
  --vnet-name vnet-hub --remote-vnet vnet-app \
  --allow-vnet-access --[[0]]
exp: The hub, which owns the gateway, sets allow-gateway-transit. The spoke side sets use-remote-gateways.

q: Choose the record type for each need.
tpl:
Route email for the domain: [[0]]
Prove domain ownership: [[1]]
Point www to app.azurewebsites.net: [[2]]
exp: MX records route mail, TXT records are used for verification, and CNAME records map one name to another.

q: Complete the statement.
tpl: A private endpoint for the blob service uses the private DNS zone [[0]].
exp: Blob private endpoints use privatelink.blob.core.windows.net. Each service has its own privatelink zone.

q: Complete the statement about Azure Load Balancer.
tpl: By default traffic is distributed with a [[0]] hash. To keep a client on the same backend VM, set session persistence to [[1]].
exp: The default uses source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port and protocol. Client IP persistence keeps a client on one backend.

q: Complete the command to enable a storage service endpoint on the subnet.
tpl:
az network vnet subnet update -g RG1 --vnet-name vnet1 -n app \
  --service-endpoints [[0]]
exp: Service endpoints are named after the resource provider, for example Microsoft.Storage or Microsoft.Sql.

q: Complete the statement about route selection.
tpl: For identical prefixes, Azure prefers [[0]] routes over BGP and system routes. Across different prefixes, the [[1]] prefix wins.
exp: Longest prefix match is applied first. For identical prefixes the order is user-defined, then BGP, then system.

q: Match each question to the Network Watcher tool.
items: Is latency to the API getting worse over time?
Which NSG rules actually apply to this NIC?
Is this specific flow allowed or denied?
Where does traffic to this address go next?
exp: Connection Monitor tracks connectivity over time; effective security rules merge NSGs; IP flow verify tests one flow; next hop shows routing.

q: Match each need to the service.
items: DNS-based global routing between regions
TCP 1433 inside a VNet
Global HTTP entry point with caching and WAF
URL path-based routing with WAF in one region
exp: Traffic Manager works through DNS; the internal LB handles private TCP; Front Door is the global HTTP edge; Application Gateway is the regional Layer 7 balancer.

q: Match each service to the subnet name it requires.
items: Azure Firewall
VPN gateway
Azure Bastion
exp: These services require dedicated subnets with exact names: Azure Firewall uses AzureFirewallSubnet, VPN and ExpressRoute gateways use GatewaySubnet, and Azure Bastion uses AzureBastionSubnet. Deployments fail if the subnet has any other name.

q: Match each outcome to the next hop type.
items: Send straight to the internet
Drop the traffic
Send to on-premises through the gateway
Send to a firewall VM
exp: Internet, None (drop), Virtual network gateway and Virtual appliance are user-defined route next-hop types.

q: Match each requirement to the connectivity option.
items: VPN from one laptop
Connect two Azure VNets over the backbone without gateways
Encrypted tunnel from an office over the internet
Private, dedicated circuit to Azure
exp: Point-to-site serves single clients; peering links VNets; site-to-site links offices; ExpressRoute is a private circuit.

q: Match each need to the DNS record.
items: Domain ownership verification
Point the apex at an Azure public IP
Delegate a subdomain
Map a host name to another name
exp: A TXT record holds verification text that proves you own a domain. An alias record lets the apex (contoso.com) point at an Azure public IP, where CNAMEs aren't allowed. An NS record delegates a subdomain to other name servers. A CNAME maps one host name to another.

q: Match each description to the feature.
items: Basic stateful allow/deny filtering on a subnet or NIC
Group NICs by application role in NSG rules
Stateful filtering with FQDN rules and threat intelligence
Microsoft-maintained groups of IP prefixes
exp: NSGs filter at Layer 3/4; ASGs group NICs; Azure Firewall adds FQDN and threat intelligence filtering; service tags represent Microsoft IP ranges.

q: Match each need to the Load Balancer feature.
items: Explicit outbound SNAT for backend VMs
Keep a client on the same backend
RDP to one specific VM through the frontend
Load-balance all ports for NVAs
exp: Outbound rules configure SNAT; session persistence keeps clients together; inbound NAT forwards to one VM; HA ports balance every port on internal load balancers.

200       Deny-Office       443   203.0.113.0/24   Deny

q: These are the inbound effective security rules on a web VM. Answer Yes or No:
stmts: A client at 203.0.113.20 can reach the VM on port 443
Another VM in the same VNet can connect on port 22
exp: Rules are processed from the lowest number. Rule 100 allows 443 from every internet address before the Deny-Office rule at 200 is reached. Only 198.51.100.10 matches the RDP rule. AllowVnetInBound permits VNet traffic on any port.

q: These are the effective routes on a VM in VNet-App. Answer Yes or No:
stmts: Traffic to 10.0.5.10 goes directly to the hub through peering
Traffic to 10.2.3.4 goes through the firewall at 10.0.1.4
Traffic to 8.8.8.8 goes directly to the internet
The system default route to the internet is invalid because a user-defined route overrides it
exp: 10.0.0.0/16 matches the peering route. 10.2.0.0/16 matches the user-defined route to the firewall. 0.0.0.0/0 points to the firewall, which replaces the default internet route.

Direction:  Inbound
Protocol:   TCP
Local:      10.2.1.5:1433
Remote:     10.1.1.4:51000
q: IP flow verify returns this result. What should you do to allow the traffic?
opts: Add a route table to the database subnet
Add an Allow rule with a lower priority number than Deny-SQL-From-Web, or change that rule
Restart the database VM
Enable a service endpoint for Microsoft.Sql
exp: IP flow verify names the NSG rule that denied the flow. Allowing it needs a higher-priority (lower-numbered) Allow rule, or a change to the deny rule.

code:
> nslookup stdata01.blob.core.windows.net
Non-authoritative answer:
Name:    stdata01.privatelink.blob.core.windows.net
Address: 10.2.4.5
Aliases: stdata01.blob.core.windows.net
q: You run this command on a VM in the VNet. What does the output show?
opts: The storage account is reached through its public endpoint
Private endpoint DNS works: the name resolves to a private IP through the privatelink zone
DNS is broken because the name changed
A service endpoint is configured
exp: The public name is a CNAME to the privatelink name, which the private DNS zone resolves to the private endpoint's IP.

q: What does this NSG rule allow?
opts: HTTP and HTTPS from the internet to NICs in the asg-web application security group
All traffic from asg-web to the internet
HTTP and HTTPS from the VNet only
Nothing, because ASGs cannot be used as destinations
exp: The rule allows inbound TCP on ports 80 and 443 from the Internet service tag to every network interface in the asg-web application security group. ASGs can be used as sources or destinations, which is the point of them. It doesn't allow outbound traffic or limit the source to the VNet.

code:
Frontend:      fe-public (Standard public IP, zone-redundant)
Backend pool:  be-web: vm1 (zone 1), vm2 (zone 2), vm3 (zone 3)
Health probe:  HTTP /health on port 80, every 5 seconds
LB rule:       TCP 80 -> 80, session persistence: None
Inbound NAT:   TCP 50001 -> vm1:3389
q: Review the load balancer configuration. Answer Yes or No:
stmts: The frontend survives the loss of one availability zone
Every request from the same client always reaches the same VM
Administrators can RDP to vm1 through the frontend on port 50001
If /health returns HTTP 500 on vm2, new connections still go to vm2
exp: A zone-redundant frontend with VMs in three zones survives a zone loss. Default distribution has no persistence. The inbound NAT rule forwards 50001 to vm1. A failing probe takes vm2 out of rotation.

q: Which statement about this private DNS zone is true?
opts: All three records were created by auto-registration
vm-web1 and vm-sql1 were created by auto-registration through a registration-enabled VNet link; api was created manually
Auto-registration is disabled for the zone
The records can be resolved from the internet
exp: AutoRegistered = True shows the record came from a registration-enabled link. Manually created records show False. Private zones resolve only inside linked VNets.

q: Why can VMs in vnet-data not reach the hub?
opts: Gateway transit is enabled
The peering has not been created on the vnet-data side yet, so its state is Initiated
Forwarded traffic is allowed
The hub has too many peerings
exp: A peering needs a link on both VNets. Initiated means only one side exists; both sides must show Connected.

q: Connection troubleshoot returns this result. What is the cause?
opts: The firewall at 10.0.1.4 drops the traffic
An NSG on the destination subnet (nsg-data) blocks the traffic
There is no route to the destination
The source VM is stopped

opts: Mail is delivered to Exchange Online, and the apex follows the pip-web IP resource
www is an alias record
The zone is private
The apex record must be updated by hand when the IP changes
exp: The MX record points to Exchange Online Protection. The apex is an alias to pip-web, so it follows IP changes. www is a CNAME.

q: Deploying Azure Bastion (Standard SKU) into this subnet fails. Why?
opts: The subnet name is wrong
The subnet is too small; AzureBastionSubnet must be /26 or larger
Bastion needs a /16 subnet
Bastion cannot be deployed in a VNet that has other subnets
exp: The subnet is named correctly (AzureBastionSubnet), but Bastion needs a /26 or larger and this one is only /27, so the deployment fails. Bastion doesn't need a /16, and it can share a VNet with other subnets.

code:
Subnet app-subnet:  natGateway = ng-out (public IP 20.50.1.1)
vm1 NIC (app-subnet): public IP 20.60.2.2
q: Which public IP does vm1 use for outbound internet connections?
opts: 20.60.2.2, the VM's own public IP
20.50.1.1, the NAT gateway's public IP
A random Azure-assigned IP
It has no outbound access
exp: NAT Gateway takes precedence for outbound traffic from its subnet, even over an instance-level public IP. The VM's own IP is still used for inbound connections.
